reason: The text survives; the citation does not. Wording and locator are sound: the sentence opens chapter I and reads exactly ‘There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.’, followed by ‘We had been wandering, indeed, in the leafless shrubbery an hour in the morning’. Attribution is Brontë’s own, on no misattribution list; shipped.js returns charlotte bronte, yearCount 2 (months 2 and 7), atCap false, banned false, shipped [], near []. What breaks it is the speaker rule. The title page is ‘Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell’: the book is framed as Jane’s own manuscript and the first sentence is her first person narration, so the speaker must be named in parentheses after the locator. The verifier applied exactly that reasoning one line earlier in this same batch, naming (Jim Burden) because ‘Cather frames the whole narrative as Jim Burden’s manuscript, so the speaker stands’, and the year’s own practice names first person narrators elsewhere (Genly Ai, Jake Barnes). Naming one and not the other is not a defensible split. A second, weaker objection, recorded rather than relied on: the line is famous as an opening and says nothing by itself, so on rule three it does little work at six in the morning on stillness and silence, and it spends Brontë’s last of three slots for the year. If the editor still wants it, ship it with the speaker named.
